Event_86_CriticalThermal.title: Emergency Thermal Shutdown (ACPI Critical Temperature Exceeded)
Event_86_CriticalThermal.description: Windows executed an emergency protective shutdown because the processor temperature reached the critical safety limit in the ACPI thermal zone. To protect the CPU and motherboard from permanent silicon damage, the kernel immediately instructed shutdown.exe to safely shut down the system.
likelyCauses: Thermal paste dried out, aged, or poorly applied between the CPU and heatsink
Cooling fan stalled, clogged with dust lint, or failing bearing
Laptop used on a soft surface (bed, blanket, lap) blocking bottom intake vents
Heatsink fins clogged with dust preventing heat dissipation
Intense sustained workload (rendering, gaming, compiling) exceeding thermal limits
remediationSteps: Surface placement: Always use the PC/laptop on a hard, flat surface or cooling pad to ensure bottom vents have unobstructed airflow.
Clear dust buildup: Use compressed air to blow out dust from intake vents and exhaust fins.
Check fan operation: Listen and feel for airflow to verify the cooling fan spins up aggressively under CPU load.

Reapply thermal paste: If the PC or laptop is more than 2 years old, dried factory thermal paste can cause 20°C+ thermal spikes. Cleaning and applying quality paste (e.g. Arctic MX-6 or Noctua NT-H2) will dramatically lower temps.
Inspect background CPU load: Open Task Manager to verify a runaway background app is not holding the CPU at 100% capacity.

Event_41_HardPowerLoss.title: Abrupt Power Loss Without Blue Screen (Event 41)
Event_41_HardPowerLoss.description: Your PC rebooted or shut down instantly without a Windows Blue Screen (BugcheckCode is 0). This means power to the motherboard cut out before Windows could even log a crash dump.
likelyCauses: Power supply (PSU) failure, over-current protection (OCP) trip, or transient power surge
Loose power cable at the back of the PC case, wall outlet, or power strip
Faulty surge protector or uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery overload
Manual hard reset (holding down the physical power button for 5+ seconds)
remediationSteps: Check physical cables: Ensure the main power cord is pressed firmly into the power supply socket and wall outlet.
Bypass power strip / UPS: Plug the PC power cord directly into a known good wall outlet to eliminate strip/surge protector faults.
Check modular PSU cables: If your power supply is modular, make sure cables (especially the 24-pin motherboard and GPU cables) are clicked tightly into the PSU chassis.
Inspect PSU capacity: If this happens while launching intensive 3D games or heavy workloads, your GPU's transient power draw may be tripping the power supply's protection circuit.
If you manually held down the power button to force a restart, this is expected behavior and not a hardware fault.

Event_41_Crash.title: Unexpected Reboot Following Blue Screen (Event 41)
Event_41_Crash.description: Your PC crashed due to a kernel stop error (Blue Screen). A crash dump was recorded before the reboot.
likelyCauses: Corrupt device driver (GPU, chipset, or storage)
Unstable memory or failing hardware component
Operating system kernel corruption
remediationSteps: Refer to the specific BugCheck code identified in the technical details below for targeted fixes.
Ensure all hardware drivers (especially graphics and chipset) are up to date.
Run System File Checker: `sfc /scannow` in an elevated command prompt.

Event_6008.title: Unexpected System Shutdown Detected (Event 6008)
Event_6008.description: The Event Log service detected that the previous shutdown at the indicated time was unexpected.
likelyCauses: System freeze, power outage, or emergency thermal shutdown
Power lost while PC was in sleep or modern standby
remediationSteps: Check if this coincided with a power outage or an Event 41 power loss.
Verify that cooling fans are spinning properly and airflow is unobstructed.
Check whether Windows Modern Standby is waking and overheating in a laptop sleeve/bag.

Event_1074.title: Normal / Planned System Shutdown (Event 1074)
Event_1074.description: The system was cleanly shut down or restarted by a user or an automated process (such as Windows Update).
likelyCauses: User clicked 'Shut down' or 'Restart' in the Start menu
Windows Update rebooted the system to apply software updates
An installer or utility triggered a clean restart
remediationSteps: No action required. This was a healthy, graceful shutdown.

Event_4101.title: Display Driver Stopped Responding and Recovered (TDR - Event 4101)
Event_4101.description: Windows detected that your graphics driver became unresponsive and successfully performed a live restart without crashing your entire PC.
likelyCauses: GPU driver crash caused by software conflict or corrupted driver files
Graphics card sagging or loose in the PCIe slot causing transient signal drops
GPU core or memory overheating under sudden graphical load
Unstable GPU clock speeds or voltage drops
remediationSteps: Clean install GPU drivers: Run Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) to wipe existing drivers, then install clean drivers from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel.
Inspect PCIe seating: Power off the PC, remove and re-seat the graphics card firmly into the PCIe slot until the retention latch snaps closed.
Check for GPU sag: If your graphics card is large or heavy, install an anti-sag support bracket to prevent PCIe pin disconnection.
Verify power: Ensure each 8-pin PCIe power connector uses a separate cable from the power supply (avoid daisy-chain pigtail cables if possible).

Event_WHEA_PCIe.title: PCI Express Bus Error Detected (WHEA-Logger)
Event_WHEA_PCIe.description: Windows Hardware Error Architecture (WHEA) reported a bus error on a PCI Express root port or endpoint (graphics card or NVMe SSD).
likelyCauses: Physical contact issue in PCIe slot (GPU sag or unseated card)
PCIe slot running at Gen 4 / Gen 5 speeds with an unstable riser cable
Dying NVMe drive controller or bad motherboard PCIe lane
remediationSteps: Reseat the graphics card: Push it firmly into the slot and screw in the bracket tightly.
Riser cable troubleshooting: If you are using a vertical GPU riser cable, enter BIOS and change PCIe speed from 'Auto/Gen 4' to 'Gen 3' to test signal stability.
Reseat NVMe SSD: Reinsert the M.2 SSD into its slot and fasten the standoff screw.
Update Motherboard BIOS to improve PCIe signal integrity microcode.

Event_37_Throttling.title: CPU Speed Limited by System Firmware (Thermal/Power Throttle)
Event_37_Throttling.description: The operating system detected that the CPU clock speed was clamped by motherboard firmware (Event 37). This typically happens when the CPU exceeds thermal thresholds or VRMs overheat.
likelyCauses: CPU thermal throttling due to insufficient cooling (dry thermal paste, failed pump, clogged dust filters)
Motherboard VRM (Voltage Regulator Module) overheating under sustained high wattage
Laptop or small-form-factor thermal constraint
remediationSteps: Check CPU cooler: If you have an All-In-One (AIO) liquid cooler, verify the pump is running and listen for water flow or gurgling.
Clean dust filters and heatsinks: Clear dust buildup from intake fans, radiator fins, and laptop vents.
Reapply thermal paste: If the PC is more than 2-3 years old, dried thermal compound can cause 20°C+ temperature spikes.
Check fan curves: Use BIOS or fan control software to ensure fans ramp up before CPU reaches 80°C.

Event_2004_OOM.title: System Ran Out of Virtual Memory (Resource Exhaustion)
Event_2004_OOM.description: Windows successfully detected a low virtual memory condition (Event 2004). Applications may crash, fail to allocate memory, or close abruptly.
likelyCauses: A background application has a severe memory leak (consuming gigabytes continuously)
Windows pagefile is disabled or manually set too small for the active workload
Too many heavy browser tabs, games, or development tools open concurrently
remediationSteps: Inspect the offending process listed in the technical details to identify which program leaked memory.

Verify pagefile settings: Press Win+R, run `sysdm.cpl`, click Advanced -> Performance Settings -> Advanced -> Virtual Memory -> Ensure 'Automatically manage paging file size for all drives' is checked.
Consider upgrading physical RAM if your regular workloads consistently exceed capacity.

Event_Storage_Error.title: Storage Controller / Disk I/O Retry Event
Event_Storage_Error.description: Windows had to retry a read/write operation to a physical storage drive or reset the storage controller.
likelyCauses: Dying SSD or hard drive with failing flash NAND or degraded platter sectors
Loose SATA data or power cable on 2.5"/3.5" drives
NVMe SSD overheating in its M.2 slot and dropping offline
remediationSteps: Back up critical personal files immediately before troubleshooting.
Inspect drive SMART health status in the Storage section of this app.
Check physical cables: If SATA, replace the SATA data cable and plug into a different motherboard SATA port.
Check NVMe thermal pad: Ensure M.2 heatsink is properly mounted to avoid thermal throttling shutdowns.

Event_1000_AppCrash.title: Application Crashed to Desktop (Event 1000)
Event_1000_AppCrash.description: An application encountered an unhandled exception and was terminated by Windows.
likelyCauses: Bug or corrupted file within the application
Conflicting overlay software (Discord overlay, RivaTuner, GeForce Experience, MSI Afterburner)
Corrupted DirectX or Visual C++ Redistributable runtime libraries
remediationSteps: Review the faulting module in the technical details to pinpoint the source (e.g., `d3d11.dll`, `vcruntime140.dll`).
Disable third-party in-game overlays (Discord, Steam, Xbox Game Bar) to test stability.
Reinstall the Microsoft Visual C++ All-In-One Redistributable packages.
Verify integrity of application files or reinstall the affected software.
